source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 8.2 Bones of the Upper Limb; 8.5

main.t: A small boat-shaped wrist bone on the thumb side of the first row of carpal bones (scaphoid).

simpler.t: The scaphoid is a small wrist bone at the base of the thumb.

deeper.t: It is one of only three carpal bones that form the wrist joint with the radius.

facts.t: It is the outermost bone of the first (proximal) row of carpal bones, on the thumb side.
Above it is the radius. Beside it, on the inner side, is the lunate.
Below it are the trapezium, trapezoid and capitate of the second row.

simpler.t: It sits in your wrist, just below the end of the forearm, on the thumb side.

deeper.t: Only the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum take part in the wrist joint.

items.name: Surface for the radius
items.t: It meets the end of the radius directly at the wrist joint.

items.name: Front (palmar) surface
items.t: It anchors the flexor retinaculum, the band that roofs the carpal tunnel.

items.name: Waist
items.t: The narrow middle part. Most fractures happen here.

simpler.t: It is small and boat-shaped, and it sits right against the end of the radius.

deeper.t: With the other carpal bones it forms the walls and floor of the carpal tunnel.

facts.t: It sits on the thumb side and meets the radius directly. So a fall on the outstretched hand drives force through it.
With the lunate and triquetrum it forms the wrist (radiocarpal) joint.
With the second row it forms the midcarpal joint. These two joints make all the movements of the wrist.

simpler.t: It helps the wrist bend and passes force from the hand to the forearm.

items.name: Wrist (radiocarpal) joint
items.t: With the lunate and triquetrum, it meets the radius here.

items.name: Midcarpal joint
items.t: The joint between the first and second rows of carpal bones.

items.name: Flexor retinaculum
items.t: Attached on the thumb side to the trapezium and scaphoid.

items.name: Radial artery
items.t: Its branches enter mainly at the far (distal) end of the scaphoid.
items.check: OpenStax traces the radial artery to the wrist; where its branches enter the scaphoid is not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–9, 12–16, 20).

items.name: Anatomical snuffbox
items.t: It lies in the floor of this hollow at the base of the thumb.

simpler.t: It forms joints with the forearm and the other wrist bones.

facts.t: It forms by replacing a cartilage model with bone (endochondral ossification), like all limb bones except the clavicle.
Its ossification centre appears in early childhood, at about five years.

items.injury: A fall onto the outstretched hand.
items.damaged: The scaphoid: the carpal bone fractured most often.
items.cannotDo: Use the wrist without deep pain on the thumb side.
items.why: Force passes from the hand to the radius through the scaphoid.

items.injury: A scaphoid fracture is missed because the first X-ray looks normal.
items.damaged: The bone itself, which has a poor blood supply.
items.cannotDo: Heal quickly: part of the bone can die (necrosis), leading later to arthritis of the wrist.
items.why: With little blood reaching it, the broken bone heals slowly.

items.q: Explain why a scaphoid fracture can be missed, and why that matters.
model: Deep pain at the outer wrist can be taken for a sprain.
The fracture may not show on an X-ray until weeks later, once swelling settles.
Its blood supply is poor, so it heals slowly.
Untreated, part of the bone can die, leading to arthritis of the wrist.

items.q: Predict which part of the scaphoid dies after a fracture across its waist, and explain why.
model: Blood vessels enter mainly at the far (distal) end.
A break across the waist cuts the near part off from its supply.

items.q: Compare a scaphoid fracture with a Colles fracture after a fall on the outstretched hand.
model: Both follow a fall onto the outstretched hand.
Scaphoid: deep pain at the outer wrist; may not show on the first X-ray.
Colles: the end of the radius breaks and is pushed backwards and upwards.
Colles gives a “dinner fork” bend just above the wrist.

check.stem: Which carpal bone is fractured most often?
check.why: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone.

check.stem: Which forearm bone does the scaphoid meet at the wrist joint?
check.why: The scaphoid and lunate meet the radius; the end of the ulna does not touch the carpal bones.

check.stem: Why can a scaphoid fracture lead to death of part of the bone?
options: It is crushed by the radius
It is pulled apart by tendons
It is too small to hold a cast
check.why: With a poor blood supply it heals slowly, and part of it can die (necrosis).
